## Abstract

Mechanisms driving aggressive meningiomas remain poorly understood. Given the pivotal role of the immune microenvironment in tumor progression, we developed a comprehensive atlas of the meningioma microenvironment, with a view toward identifying modifiable opportunities.

The immune microenvironment of 2,727 meningiomas was profiled using orthogonal methodologies, including 24 with mass cytometry, 24 single-cell RNAseq, 1,437 bulk RNAseq, 1,125 DNA methylation, 117 multiplex immunofluorescence, as well as that of 5 paired peripheral blood samples and 10 human meninges. Patient-derived organotypic tumor spheroids (PDOTS) were established to assess the effect of STING stimulation combined with anti-PD-1 treatment.

We revealed a rich immune infiltration in meningioma, among the highest across 34 human cancer types (n = 12,188). Macrophages predominated in meningioma microenvironment, in contrast to the lymphoid dominance of peripheral blood, with meninges exhibiting an intermediate immune profile between meningiomas and peripheral blood. Cellular states and phenotypes of both immune and tumor cells shifted during tumor progression, with aggressive meningiomas possessing earlier-stage, immunosuppressive immune cells and proliferative tumor cells. Using ex vivo meningioma PDOTS, we demonstrated inducible responses to STING activation, marked by elevated cytokine release, which were synergistic when combined with PD-1 blockade.

These findings offer an extensive resource on the cellular heterogeneity of the meningioma microenvironment and provide a framework for rational therapeutic modeling and strategy development.

Keywords: cell differentiation, immune microenvironment, macrophage, meningioma, STING

- Meningiomas exhibit robust immune infiltration, compared to 30+ other human tumor types.

- Aggressive meningiomas possess less-differentiated immune and tumor cells.

- Combining STING agonist and PD-1 blockade may be synergistic in treating aggressive meningiomas.

Importance of the Study

Aggressive meningiomas, the most common primary central nervous system tumor, lack effective therapeutic targets. Given the meninges’ role as an immune gateway and the growing evidence linking tumor progression to immune infiltration, we comprehensively mapped the meningioma microenvironment using single-cell and bulk genomic profiling. Analysis of 2,727 meningiomas revealed a robust immune infiltration—among the highest across 34 human cancer types—highlighting a potential application of immune-directed therapies in meningioma. The meninges displayed an intermediate immune profile between meningiomas and peripheral blood, and intratumoral immune and tumor cells occupied immunosuppressive and proliferative states in aggressive meningiomas. Using patient-derived organotypic tumor spheroids, STING activation triggered potent cytokine release, synergizing with PD-1 blockade. Our study underlines the rich immune milieu in meningioma, with differences across biological states, and provides a framework for advancing treatment strategies for aggressive subtypes.

The rise of widespread molecular profiling for meningioma, the most common central nervous system (CNS) tumor in adults, has unveiled a complex genomic landscape underlying these tumors.1–5 Multimodal technologies, including targeted gene sequencing, whole-genome microarray, and DNA methylation profiling, have revealed significant genomic divergence across clinical phenotypes.1–3,5–8 The discovery of oncogenic drivers beyond NF2 loss raised hopes for targeted therapies for meningiomas.9–11 However, mutational changes that are candidates for currently available therapeutic targeting are predominantly observed in lower grade meningiomas and are notably rare in more aggressive cases.12 Instead, higher grade meningiomas are characterized by extensive chromosomal copy number alterations (CNAs)4,5,12 and epigenetic signatures.2,6,7 These features, combined with substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity in aggressive meningiomas, have hindered the development of effective therapeutic options for patients with these tumors.13,14

Given the genomic variability among tumors, the immune compartment has emerged as a potentially modifiable therapeutic avenue.15,16 Contemporary molecular classification systems also increasingly recognize immune phenotypes as an attribute of meningiomas.1–3,6 Additionally, growing evidence suggest an association between increased tumor cell aneuploidy, reflected by broad CNAs, and immune evasion, which further highlights modulation of the immune microenvironment as an appealing strategy for meningiomas.17

Here, we sought to define the immune microenvironment of meningiomas by applying orthogonal methodologies across institutional and publicly available datasets. Our findings reveal a rich, context-dependent immune environment in nearly every profiled meningioma and highlight molecular targets that may represent novel strategies for durable immune modulation.

## Methods

### Cohort

We analyzed 2,727 meningioma samples from our institute and publicly available databases to profile the immune landscape of human meningiomas (Table 1) and explore its therapeutic implications. We first profiled 56 meningiomas surgically resected at Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH) between 2008 and 2021. Twenty-four specimens were profiled by mass cytometry (cytometry by time-of-flight, CyTOF), 8 by single cell RNAseq (scRNAseq), and 47 by bulk RNAseq (15 of which also underwent CyTOF, and 8 scRNAseq). Demographic and clinical data were extracted from the institutional electronic medical record. For the majority of cases from public datasets, the 2016 WHO classification was used due to a lack of available molecular data.18 When the current 2021 WHO classification was available (institutional cases), this was used. Mitoses per 10 high-powered fields and CNAs from whole-genome microarrays (Affymetrix Oncoscan) were extracted to calculate a molecularly Integrated Grade.3 A methylation class2 was assigned to 185 meningiomas with both bulk RNAseq and DNA methylation profiling (GSE183653) and 24 tumors with scRNAseq data.

We developed an extrapolation cohort to validate observations about the immune landscape in meningioma and its clinical implications. We incorporated meningiomas with available sequencing data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository, including 16 specimens with scRNAseq, 1,390 with bulk RNAseq, 1,125 with bulk DNA methylation profiling data, as well as a tissue microarray (TMA) with 117 meningiomas (Table 1). Available clinical information was extracted from associated publications.1,2,13,19–26

### Mass Cytometry (CyTOF)

Meningioma tissues were processed for CyTOF within 30 minutes of being surgically resected, as detailed in the ­Supplementary Methods. To investigate the differential immune compositions between the peripheral circulation and meningiomas, we also processed the paired blood of 5 meningiomas using published protocols.27

Two CyTOF marker panels were designed (Table S1). Staining of the surface and intracellular CyTOF antibodies was conducted in accordance with previously described protocols27–29 (Supplementary Methods).

Cytometry by time-of-flight for meningioma and paired blood samples were done using the Helios CyTOF System (Fluidigm). Data were acquired in the FCS file format and imported into CytoBank website (https://premium.cytobank.org/). We manually removed beads from all events, isolated cells using the embedded EQ beads (a set of polystyrene microbeads), gated singlets with DNA1/DNA2 channels, and excluded dead cells based on the viability staining with 195Pt isotope. Filtered data were exported into R for further analysis (Supplementary Methods).

### Single-Cell RNA Sequencing

Single-cell RNA sequencing for 8 meningioma specimens was performed at the BWH Single-cell Genomics Core, using sample preparation protocols as previously described.30,31 We also identified 28 meningiomas with scRNAseq files from 5 datasets in GEO (GSE234402, GSE213544, GSE183655, GSE256490, and GSE206647). After screening sample quality, we included 16 samples (GSE206647)32 in our analysis which passed quality metrics. We generated meningioma-specific immune signatures (LM11 matrix, Table S2) from these scRNAseq datasets with 1,778 genes. Data processing and further analysis of the immune microenvironment are available in Supplementary Methods.

### Human Meninges

To investigate the cellular immune microenvironment of meninges and its relationship to the peripheral blood and meningiomas, we analyzed 10 normal human meninges samples with scRNAseq: 1 arachnoid from a patient with a resected arachnoid cyst from BWH and 9 dura mater from previously published works (2 from GEO-GSE1836552, and 7 from Zenodo files [10.5281/zenodo.4932158]33).

### Bulk RNA Sequencing

Fresh frozen meningioma tissues were acquired from 47 meningiomas resected at BWH and sent for bulk RNAseq at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. To expand our institutional cohort, we included another 1,390 meningioma samples with bulk RNAseq data from the GEO database (Table 1). Gene count matrices of specimens were imported into R, and quanTIseq34 was utilized to infer the global immune fraction within the tumor mass. Cibersort35 was used to characterize the cellular composition of meningiomas, applying the meningioma-specific scRNAseq-based LM11 matrix (Supplementary Methods).

For the pan-cancer immune analyses, we acquired bulk RNAseq datasets of 33 tumor types from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database. For immune identity profiling, we applied the LM22 matrix containing leukocyte signatures based on 547 genes (https://github.com/SiYangming/CIBERSORT-DATA/blob/main/LM22.txt).

### DNA Methylation Profiling

We included 1,125 meningiomas with available bulk DNA methylation data (Table 1) and applied MethylResolver36 to deconvolute estimated fractions of immune cell types within the tumor microenvironment as well as tumor purity.

### Cell Differentiation Analysis

CytoTrace is a computational framework to infer cell differentiation by calculating the number of detectably expressed genes, with the premise that gene counts decrease with successive stages of cell development.37 With CytoTrace2,38 we elucidated the differentiation states of immune and tumor cells within meningiomas using scRNAseq data.

Monocle39 analyzes single-cell gene expression and orders cells along a trajectory corresponding to the process of cell development. We further clustered pseudotime-dependent genes and plotted on heatmaps, with corresponding clinical features annotated on ridge plots.

Slingshot,40 RNA velocity,41 and expression analysis of progenitor/stem cell-like genes were also adopted in this study. Details are available in the Supplementary Methods.

### Cell-Cell Interaction Analysis

To infer the directionality and strength of intercellular connections, we applied CellCall42 and CellChat43 to scRNAseq data. Additionally, we inferred cellular interactions on a TMA of meningiomas using Orion, a high-plex imaging method designed for the simultaneous detection of multiple protein markers in a single tissue section.44

### Immunohistochemistry

Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue-microarray slides from patients with brain tumors were purchased from Biomax (GL2082) and used for the immunohistochemistry of the stimulator of interferon genes (STING) performed on the Leica Bond III automated staining platform, as previously published.45 The antibody for STING (Cell Signaling Technology #13647, clone D2P2F) was run at 1:50 dilution with the Leica Biosystems Refine Detection Kit with citrate antigen retrieval. Immunohistochemistry staining was quantified in QuPath (0.2.0-m4).46 Immunopositivity was quantified with default settings for 3,3′-diaminobenzidine staining to detect positive pixels in randomly selected fields across each tumor, which were then averaged. Data for astrocytoma (including glioblastoma), oligodendroglioma, and normal brain were previously published45 and are included for comparison with the meningioma staining.

### Patient-Derived Organotypic Tumor Spheroids and Cytokine Assays

Fresh meningioma tumor tissue (refrigerated but not frozen and studied within 24 hours of collection) was used for cytokine analysis, as previously described.47 Briefly, resected meningioma specimens (n = 6) were minced with prewarmed (37°C) media (DMEM from Thermo Fisher Scientific #10013CV, 10% FBS, 100 U/mL collagenase type IV [Thermo Fisher Scientific #17104019] and 50 μg/mL DNase I [Roche #10104159001]) for 20 minutes. Tumor spheroids were subsequently maintained in ultralow-attachment tissue culture plates (Corning) in DMEM (4.5 mM glucose, 100 mM Na pyruvate, 1:100 penicillin-streptomycin; Corning CellGro). These patient-derived organotypic tumor spheroids were treated with ADU-S100 (50 μM), nivolumab (100 μg/mL), combined treatment, or distilled water (dH2O) control.

Cytokine concentration was assessed using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA, R&D Systems) according to the manufacturer’s instructions on the conditioned media collected from cell culture. C-X-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 10 (CXCL10) was assessed on day 3 for all patients and on day 6 for patients 4-6. Multiplexed cytokine analysis was performed on day 6 for patients 4-5 using a bead-based immunoassay approach with the Bio-Plex Pro Human Cytokine 40-plex Assay (Cat. #171AK99MR2) on a Bio-Plex 200 system (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Cat. #171000201) and the Human Cytokine/Chemokine Magnetic Bead Panel (Cat. #HCYTMAG-60K-PX30) on a Luminex MAGPIX system (Merck Millipore) (Supplementary Methods).

### Statistical Analyses

Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 26.0.0.0), R (version 4.3.1), and GraphPad Prism (version 9.5.0). The t-test or nonparametric Mann-Whitney test was used, depending on data distribution, to compare quantitative parameters between two groups. Ordinary one-way ANOVA, corrected for multiple comparisons by controlling the false discovery rate, or the Kruskal-Wallis test was employed for comparisons among three or more groups. Statistical significance was defined as a two-sided P-value (<.05).

## Results

### Multimodal Profiling Reveals a Rich Immune Microenvironment in Meningioma

We observed a robust immune compartment across 2,727 meningiomas (64% WHO grade 1, 29% WHO grade 2, 7% WHO grade 3), profiled through single-cell (24 CyTOF and 24 scRNAseq) and bulk methodologies (1,437 bulk RNAseq and 1,125 DNA methylation profiling), with validation on another 117 meningiomas in TMA (Figure 1A, Table 1). Despite variability in the proportion of immune cells across samples, nearly all tumors exhibited an immune signature (Figure 1B-F). Immune cell estimates differed by methodology, with bulk RNA sequencing identifying a median of 40% of tumor mass (IQR 27%-60%), compared to a median of 21% (IQR 17%-26%) from DNA methylation analyses (P < .001, Figure 1B and C). At the single-cell level, we identified 59,867 PTPRC-expressing leukocytes from 115,586 cells across 24 meningiomas using transcriptomic sequencing and 55,322 CD45+ immune cells among 77,498 cells from another 24 meningiomas using mass cytometry (Figure 1D and E). This immune-rich milieu in meningioma was exceeded only by hematologic cancers (lymphoma and leukemia) and tumors of the thymus, a lymphoid organ, when we assessed the abundance of immune infiltrates in 12,188 human tumors spanning 34 cancer types with bulk RNAseq (Figure 1G).

The relative compositions of distinct immune cell lineages were consistent across all transcriptomic and proteomic platforms, despite methodological differences in the ­absolute or inferred immune cell fraction (Figures S1-S3, Figure 1H and I). Myeloid lineage cells predominated over lymphoid cells, and a significant presence of both lineages existed alongside tumor cells in all single-cell-profiled meningiomas.

We applied a methylation-based classification2 to 185 meningiomas with both DNA methylation and RNAseq profiling and observed a similar trend of significantly higher inferred immune fraction from RNAseq data compared to methylation data (Figure S4). Although the methylation-based immune-enriched subgroup expressed the highest average immune fraction (51% inferred from RNAseq and 25% from methylation), the merlin-intact and hypermitotic meningiomas demonstrated significant immune cell fractions of 40%-44% based on bulk RNAseq and 18%-19% based on DNA methylation (P < .05), respectively (Figure S4A and B). Notably, myeloid cells dominated the microenvironment of the immune-enriched meningiomas, while lymphoid cells waned compared to the other two groups (Figure S4C).

Tumor biology influenced intratumoral immune infiltration. Among meningioma tissue samples profiled with multiplex immunofluorescence, an immune presence was appreciable across each WHO grade, with the largest fractions present in grade 1 and 2 meningiomas (Figure 1J). A similar trend was observed when assessing meningiomas using the molecularly Integrated Grade,3 derived from CNAs and mitotic count (Figure 1K). NF2 loss was detected in 34 of 47 institutional patients (72%) with bulk RNAseq, with NF2-loss meningiomas exhibiting comparable immune infiltration patterns to NF2-intact meningiomas (Figure S5).

### Macrophages Dominate the Meningioma Immune Environment

To further elucidate the cellular composition of meningiomas, we constructed a high-resolution atlas using 48 tumors with single-cell profiling data (Figure 2A-D). Transcriptomic analyses of 115,586 cells from 24 meningiomas with scRNAseq identified 25 clusters, which were consolidated into 11 major cell types: myeloid-lineage cells (macrophages, neutrophils, and other myeloid cells), lymphoid-lineage cells (CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, NK cells, and B cells), and non-immune cells (meningioma cells, endothelial cells, pericytes, and oligodendrocytes) (Figure 2A and B, Figure S1). Within the non-immune compartment, approximately 5% of cells expressed endothelial, epithelial, or oligodendroglial markers, with the remainder inferred as tumor cells. Tumor cell identity was then validated by the expression of meningioma-specific transcription factors (Figure S6)48 and by the detection of chromosomal copy number variations (Figure S7). Of note, OLIG1-expressing cells were detected in 8 samples with scRNAseq data, and 93% of these cells were from WHO grade 2 and 3 meningiomas, indicative of brain invasion. Single-cell mass cytometry of an independent cohort of 24 meningiomas (77,498 cells) validated similar immune and non-immune cell clusters while highlighting the diversity of the immune compartment (Figure 2C and D, Figure S2).

Macrophages, including microglia (Figure S8), represented the majority of the immune cells in meningiomas, followed by T cells, with NK cells, B cells, neutrophils, and others comprising a minority fraction, as revealed by single-cell profiling (Figure 2E). This was corroborated through deconvolution of bulk genomic sequencing data from 2,562 meningiomas ­(Figure 2F). On pan-cancer analysis, meningiomas exhibited one of the highest macrophage-to-T cell ratios across 34 tumor types (Figure 2G).

The relative abundance of immune cell types varied with clinical characteristics across meningiomas profiled through bulk and single-cell modalities (Figure 2H-J, Table 1). Among 1,428 meningiomas with available WHO grade annotation, the proportion of macrophages in the tumor microenvironment decreased with increasing grade: WHO grade 3 meningiomas displayed a smaller proportion of macrophages (61%) compared to WHO grade 1 (68%, P < .001) and grade 2 (65%, P = .04) tumors (Figure 2H). Conversely, higher-grade meningiomas had a greater proportion of T cells within the immune compartment (WHO grade 3 vs. grade 1: P = .02, grade 2 vs. grade 1: P < .001, Figure 2H). Macrophage fractions also varied by tumor status, with recurrent meningiomas (n = 90) having a smaller proportion of macrophages (58%) compared to primary tumors (n = 302, 66%, Figure 2I). Radiation exposure also altered the immune composition, with irradiated meningiomas (n = 32) having a higher fraction of NK cells and a lower fraction of B cells compared to non-radiated tumors (n = 255, Figure 2J).

### Early-Stage, Immune-Suppressive Macrophages Accumulate in Aggressive Meningiomas

To better understand the role of macrophages—the dominant immune population in meningioma—we investigated changes in their developmental states and cellular phenotypes across tumor grade. Analysis of 24 tumors with scRNAseq data revealed that macrophages in aggressive meningiomas exhibit less differentiated and more immune-regulatory characteristics (Figure 3).

Using CytoTrace,37 we calculated potency scores for each macrophage (Figure 3A and Figure S9A and B). Higher absolute and relative potency scores indicated higher developmental potential and less differentiated states. When ranked by potency scores, high-grade, recurrent, and metastatic meningiomas were significantly enriched with high-score macrophages compared to the lower-grade and primary tumors (all P < .001, Figure 3A). Relative potency scores further confirmed that macrophages from aggressive meningiomas were clustered within less-differentiated groups with higher potency scores (Figure S9A and B).

The above findings were verified with an independent method, Monocle,39 which orders cells along a biological progression trajectory. Early-stage macrophages were predominantly associated with WHO grade 3, recurrent, and metastatic meningiomas and showed elevated expression of ID2, BIRC3, SOCS3, REL, and NAMPT (Figure 3B-D). By contrast, lower-grade and primary meningiomas were characterized by late-stage macrophages.

Further, we leveraged RNA velocity41 analysis to derive pseudotime scores, ranging from 0 (less differentiated) to 1 (more differentiated), and a dynamical model to compute kinetics-based latent time scores on the same scale. In both analyses, macrophages from grade 1 meningiomas exhibited higher pseudotime and latent time compared to grade 2-3 meningiomas (P < .001, Figure 3E and F), consistent with a more differentiated state of macrophage.

Gene expression-based phenotypic analyses revealed an enrichment of stress-tolerant, immune-suppressive, and proliferative macrophage subpopulations in aggressive meningiomas (Table S3). Among the ten identified macrophage clusters, immune-suppressive (M5), stress-adaptative (M8), and proliferative (M9) phenotypes, as defined by marker genes reported in the literature,49–51 were more abundant in WHO grade 3 and metastatic meningiomas (P < .05, Figure 3G and H, Figure S9C). These subpopulations exhibited higher potency scores, indicating relatively less differentiated states (Figure S9D-F).

### Aggressive Meningiomas Harbor Less-Differentiated, Immune-Regulatory T Cells

Similar to macrophages, scRNAseq analysis on 13,742 T cells revealed that less-differentiated, immune-suppressive T cells were enriched in higher-grade, recurrent, and metastatic meningiomas (Figures S9 and S10). Estimation and ranking of T cell developmental potentials revealed that earlier stage T cells made up only 7% of all T cells, and most of these cells were attributed to WHO grade 3, recurrent, and metastatic tumors (Figure S10A and B). Absolute potency comparisons across WHO grade and tumor states, as well as visualization on relative-scoring plots, confirmed that T cells in aggressive tumors are predominantly in early-differentiation stages (all P < .001, Figures S9G-K and S10C).

Pseudotime trajectory supported above findings, with T cells from aggressive tumors located at early developmental stages, characterized by the expression of IL7R, JUND, PTMA, ARID5B, and SRGN (Figure S10D-F). By contrast, T cells from benign and untreated tumors were positioned at later developmental stages.

We next interrogated the identity of T cells using gene expression analysis and identified nine distinct phenotypes (Figure S10G and H). WHO grade 3 and metastatic tumors were enriched with T cells from four specific subpopulations (Table S4)52–57: T0 (naïve/memory), T6 (tissue-resident), T7 (regulatory), and T8 (proliferative). These groups exhibited the highest potency scores and were enriched with less-differentiated T cells (Figure S10G-J).

This early-stage state of macrophages and T cells in aggressive meningiomas was further validated through mapping of cell identity branching trajectories using Slingshot (Figure S11A),40 multiplex immunofluorescence staining (Figure S11B and C), and single-cell gene expression analysis (Figure S11D). Bulk RNAseq analysis also corroborated the up-regulation of early-stage, immune-regulatory gene signatures in higher-grade (175 WHO grade 2-3 vs. 345 WHO grade 1) and recurrent (56 vs. 214 primary) meningiomas (Figure S12, Table S5).

### Tumor Cell States Evolve With Meningioma Aggressiveness

Each meningioma exhibited a clearly defined tumor cell ­differentiation state, different from the immune lineages (Figure S13A and B). Analysis of 51,802 tumor cells revealed that less-differentiated subpopulations were strongly associated with higher grade, recurrent, and metastatic meningiomas (Figure S13C). Tumor cells exhibited a broader range of potency scores compared to immune cells, reflecting their potential for rapid proliferation and differentiation (Figures S13C vs. S3A and S10C). Monocle pseudotime trajectory indicated that tumor cells from aggressive meningiomas were of early stages of cell development (Figure S13D), characterized by proliferative and genomically unstable phenotypes (Figure S13E-G) and high potency scores (Figure S13H and I). CyTOF analysis confirmed that grade 3 and recurrent meningiomas had a significantly higher fraction of Nestin-positive tumor cells, indicating a stem-like subpopulation that may drive tumor growth (Figure S13J and K).

### Intratumoral Cellular Interactions Indicate Macrophage-Tumor Cell Communications

Meningioma microenvironment displayed complex interactions between macrophage-tumor, macrophage-macrophage, and tumor-tumor cells (Figures S14 and S3I-K). Using CellCall42 and CellChat,43 we inferred from scRNAseq data the directionality and strength of intercellular connections. We observed these connections to be most prominent between macrophages and tumor cells, as well as tumor-tumor cells and macrophages-macrophages (Figures S14A-C and S3I). Multiplex immunofluorescence of meningioma TMA corroborated this result, with the highest spatial coupling observed between SIX1+ tumor cells and CD68+/CD163+ macrophages (Figure 3I-K, Figure S14D and E). Moreover, tumor cells exhibited activation of Hippo, MAPK, and FoxO signaling pathways (P < .01), while both macrophages and tumor cells influenced cell adhesion. For macrophages, pathways such as adipocytokine and TNF pathways were exclusively activated by immune cells, while NF-κB-related immune responses were primarily stimulated by T cells (Figure S14B and C).

### Immune Cell Lineages Differ Across Meningioma Grade

We next explored the phenotypes and origins of immune cell lineages. Given the interplay between the tumor microenvironment and systemic compartments, we analyzed paired meningioma and peripheral blood samples using CyTOF, revealing differences in the dominant immune cell lineages between the tumor mass and circulation (Figure 4).

Across all samples (with 41,341 cells), T cells were the predominant immune cells in the peripheral blood, whereas macrophages dominated in meningiomas (Figure 4A and B). Differences also emerged in immune cell characterization: T cells occupied a helper phenotype in blood compared to a cytotoxic profile within tumor microenvironment, while macrophages in tumor exhibited a more homeostatic, immune-surveillance profile (Figure 4C-E). In the peripheral blood, CD4 T cells were the predominant subpopulation, with a CD4/CD8 ratio >1 in all samples (range 1.4-5.8). However, this ratio reversed in the tumor microenvironment, where CD8 T cells predominated (CD4/CD8: 0.4-0.8, P = .001; Figure 4C).

Among macrophages, clustering with CyTOF markers revealed that 75% of peripheral monocytes/macrophages exhibited a pro-inflammatory phenotype with high Ki-67/CD86/CD192 expression (C9 cluster, Figure 4D and E). In contrast, macrophages within meningiomas predominantly displayed an immune-suppressive profile, with 50% falling into clusters characterized by high expression of immunosuppressive markers such as OX40L, TIM-3, PD-1, and CD73 (C2 cluster) or HLA-G, B7-H3, CD39, PD-L1, and PD-L2 (C4 cluster; Figure 4D and E). Regarding origin, the peripheral macrophages were likely bone marrow derived (CD192/CD86) while the intratumoral macrophages were enriched for tissue-resident origins (Figure 4D-F). Notably, macrophage origin differed also by tumor grade: WHO grade 3 meningiomas (n = 3, with 3,326 cells) recruited more bone marrow-derived CD192/CD86 cells and expressed lower levels of PU.1 compared to grade 1 (n = 12, with 26,352 cells) or grade 2 (n = 9, with 10,906 cells) tumors (P < .001, Figure 4F).

Human meninges displayed an “intermediate” immune state between the systemic and tumor immune compositions. We observed a rich endogenous immune microenvironment within human meninges on scRNAseq analysis of 26,030 cells (9 dura, 1 arachnoid), with arachnoid having a relatively greater immune infiltration compared to dura ­(Figure 4G and H). A stepwise decrease in lymphoid cells and a corresponding increase in myeloid cells was observed from peripheral blood to normal meninges to meningiomas, suggesting an intermediate immunologic state in normal meninges (all P < .01, Figure 4I). Furthermore, macrophage lineages varied between meningeal layers, with dura containing less-differentiated macrophages primarily of bone marrow origin, while arachnoid harbored more-differentiated, tissue-resident macrophages (Figure S15). These findings infer the context-dependent immune landscape of meningiomas, revealing differences between tumor, systemic, and meningeal immune environments.

### Multimodal Profiling Identifies Potential Immunotherapeutic Targets for Meningioma

Building on the immune cell composition and interaction landscape of meningiomas, we next explored therapeutic targets for immune modulation (Figure 5). We observed robust expression of STING in macrophages (80%) and tumor cells (60%), followed by CD73 and B7-H3, as inferred from CyTOF and scRNAseq (Figure 5A and B). Across immune checkpoint markers, which have been therapeutically targeted with initial promise in some patients with aggressive meningiomas,15,58 PD-1 protein was expressed in 37% of T cells on CyTOF (SD: 22%, Figure 5A), although it constituted only a minor fraction of the total tumor microenvironment (Figure 5B).

For three patients with recurrent WHO grade 3 meningiomas treated with nivolumab (a PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor) prior to resection,15 PD-1 expression on T cells was significantly lower compared to non-nivolumab treated controls (Figure 5C). Additionally, PD-1 blockade may also influence the expression of a range of immune signatures compared to a control group of recurrent, grade 2-3 meningiomas with prior radiation treatment (Figure 5D). Despite the efficacy of lowering expression of PD-1 and several other immune-suppressive immune checkpoints, all three patients experienced disease progression within 3-7 months of treatment.

These patient outcomes prompted our search for therapeutic strategies to work in tandem with PD-1 blockade. STING emerged as a promising candidate due to its robust expression across cell lineages in meningiomas, its enrichment compared to gliomas and normal brain tissue (Figures S16 and S5A, B, and E), and its ability to foster downstream activation of anti-tumoral immune cells.59,60 Further, STING expression increased with tumor grade (Figure 5F) and with recurrence in four patients with serial resection of high-grade meningioma (Figure 5G). Despite this grade-dependent increase, downstream interferon signaling did not appear basally active in scRNAseq analysis of STING-related pathways (Figure 5H), suggesting that while the STING pathway is transcriptionally primed, it is functionally dormant. We therefore explored the application of a STING agonist, ADU-S100, to induce cytokine activation independently and in conjunction with PD-1 blockade.

As patient samples most faithfully recapitulate the tumor immune microenvironment, we investigated STING as a therapeutic target in freshly resected meningiomas. We applied ADU-S100 to ex vivo organoids established from six human meningiomas. Following treatment, we observed successful induction of CXCL10, a chemokine that contributes to the generation of a “hot” tumor immune microenvironment,61 from day 3 through day 6 (Figure 5I). Notably, combining PD-1 inhibition via nivolumab with the STING agonist led to more robust chemokine release, suggesting a potential role for combinatorial immunotherapeutic strategies in meningioma treatment (Figure 5I and J).

## Discussion

Effective therapeutic targets are needed for aggressive meningiomas, the most common primary CNS tumors. Given the pivotal role of immune infiltration in the tumorigenesis and progression of brain tumors62,63 and increasing recognition of the meninges as a gateway for systemic immune entry into the brain,64,65 we aimed to develop a comprehensive atlas of the meningioma microenvironment by combining single-cell and bulk genomic profiling. This work maps a rich cellular diversity within meningiomas and explores the association of immune signatures with tumor biology and therapeutic potential.

Our findings demonstrate a robust overall immune infiltration across meningiomas. Studies drawing from bulk analysis with whole-genome sequencing, DNA methylation, and epigenetic profiling have highlighted the enrichment of immune signatures in a subset of meningiomas, often with benign genomic characteristics.1–3,6 This aligns with our findings that low-grade meningiomas exhibit greater immune cell infiltration relative to higher-grade meningiomas. Nevertheless, even high-grade meningiomas exhibited prominent immune infiltration within the tumor microenvironment, underscoring meningioma as one of the most immune-rich human tumors.

Immune population analysis revealed macrophages as the dominant immune cells in meningiomas, consistent with prior studies on meningiomas66 and other primary brain tumors.67 This contrasts with extracranial cancers68–71 and brain metastases,72 where T cells are more abundant. Interestingly, while the absolute immune-to-tumor cell fraction varied across methodological platforms, the relative immune composition remained consistent, ensuring reliable interpretation of immune profiles in meningioma. Future studies on such methodologic impact will be needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying these deconvolution differences.

The distinct landscape of meningiomas may be attributed to their origin within the meninges. Recent studies have reframed the meninges, particularly the dura and arachnoid, as an immune organ rather than a simple physical barrier covering the brain.2,33 We observed the meninges to exhibit an intermediate immune profile between that of meningiomas and peripheral blood. Therefore, we conceptualize meningiomas as a microcosm of dynamically regulated tumor and immune cells, which may derive from both local and systemic sources.

We also observed a progressive de-differentiation of both immune and tumor cells during meningioma progression. Well-differentiated, immune-active T cells and macrophages transitioned into less-differentiated, immune-regulatory phenotypes in malignant meningiomas. Tumor cells similarly acquired less-developed, stem-like characteristics, reflecting convergence of immune and tumor cell evolution during disease progression. These phenotypic shifts parallel findings in other cancers and highlight the dynamic and adaptive nature of the tumor microenvironment.73–75

Our study identifies potential therapeutic targets for meningiomas. The robust immune signatures and intercellular communication networks suggest opportunities for pathway-specific interventions. However, the overall immune-suppressive milieu in aggressive meningiomas may pose a barrier to effective immune-based therapies in aggressive meningiomas, despite the fact that several well-characterized immunomodulatory markers were robustly observed. We highlighted synergistic potential between combinatorial immunotherapies by inducing STING activation to augment the impact of anti-PD-1 treatment, consistent with findings reported in other cancers.76 The abundant expression of STING on both macrophages and meningioma tumor cells, as well as its persistent, and even elevated, expression with recurrence and malignancy, poises STING targeting as a promising primer of immune activation in meningiomas.15,16,77,78

Lastly, the immense immune presence and its ability to change with biological behavior argue for the need to incorporate the tumor microenvironment background in models of meningioma for therapeutic testing. Existing cell lines for meningioma largely fail to recapitulate the genomic characteristics of human meningioma,79 and primary cultures of patient-derived meningioma lines are challenging to maintain. Animal models are stratified between genetically engineered models or orthotopic injections of established meningioma cell lines,80 where the impact of immune modulation remains to be established. Patient-derived ex vivo organoids81 and naturally occurring canine meningiomas82,83 may offer a natural immunologic milieu that supports cross-talk with tumor cells.

One limitation of our study is the lack of uniform WHO grading available, stemming from the absence of comprehensive molecular data from public datasets. The 2021 WHO classification was applied for institutional cases with detailed molecular profiling, while the 2016 metrics were used for publicly available cohorts. Moreover, trajectory inference in immune cells is indirect and algorithm-dependent and will be strengthened by future functional validation. Finally, while exploration of STING agonist supports the utility of an immune profiling framework for therapeutic exploration, further studies are needed to validate its translational potential in patients.

Altogether, this study provides an extensive resource detailing the cellular heterogeneity of the meningioma tumor microenvironment, encompassing immune phenotypes, cellular states, and signaling pathways. These insights provide a foundational framework for developing rational models and advancing therapeutic strategies for this common yet challenging tumor.

# Corticobulbar Motor Evoked Potentials: A Systematic Review of Technical Variations

**Authors:** Casey A Jarvis; Matthew Toczylowski; Mitali Bose; Ruchit V Patel; Julia Wang; James Tanner McMahon; Wenya Linda Bi

## Abstract

Corticobulbar motor evoked potentials (coMEPs) were introduced in 2005 as an alternative to direct stimulation and free running electromyography for continuous monitoring of the facial nerve during skull base surgery. The technique has been expanded for monitoring of multiple cranial nerves (CNs) and adapted across diverse pathologies. Nonetheless, broad adoption has lagged. This study aimed to understand the basis of this disparity by systematically mapping current practices and characterizing the variations in technical implementation and reporting of coMEPs.

We conducted a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 adherent systematic review of all articles reporting coMEP neuromonitoring published through December 6, 2023. Multiple reviewers screened publications for inclusion. Data were extracted using a standardized template to enable quantitative and qualitative data synthesis. Aggregate data were analyzed to address incidence, reporting variability, and sensitivity/specificity of the method.

We identified 2711 unique cases using coMEPs, reported across 72 studies (2005-2023). Significant heterogeneity was observed in the technique of coMEPs, including stimulation montages and measurements of accuracy. Overall, 81.9% (59/72) of studies reported clinical outcomes, whereas the remainder were technically focused. coMEPs were often used alongside other neuromonitoring modalities (87.5% of studies, 63/72), but performance was directly compared only 25% of the time (18/72). The facial nerve was the most common single target analyzed (n = 41 publications), followed by the vagus (n = 9). Twenty-two percent of studies analyzed multiple CNs (n = 16). Less than 50% of facial nerve studies, and no vagal nerve study, reported sensitivity or specificity of coMEPs.

coMEPs are an evolving technique in intraoperative neuromonitoring, powerful for their continuous monitoring of the entire motor pathways involving a CN. Comparison of the sensitivity and specificity of coMEPs to other modalities was limited by inconsistent reporting, highlighting the need for further investigation and prospective studies. Standardization of technique may facilitate broader adoption and acceptance of coMEPs.

Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) of cranial nerves (CNs) was developed in the 1960s to reduce facial nerve injury during vestibular schwannoma resection.1 Direct or triggered electromyography (EMG) and free running EMG were the original monitoring modalities introduced. Triggered EMG allows the operator to locate the course of a nerve intraoperatively and assess nerve function on demand; it relies on direct stimulation, thereby providing intermittent feedback (Figure 1). Continuous triggered EMG was subsequently developed to address this limitation, although it still requires exposure of the nerve, which may be challenging in some cases.2 Free-running EMG also provides continuous monitoring, however, it relies on irritation of the nerve and is subject to significant artifact. In addition, only select muscles may fire with any of these modalities, with the risk of false negatives.

Corticobulbar motor evoked potentials (coMEPs) were introduced in 20053,4 as an alternative to direct stimulation and free-running EMGs for facial nerve monitoring during skull base surgery. coMEPs enable continuous monitoring of facial functional integrity from the motor cortex to the neuromuscular junction, without the need for nerve exposure (Figure 1). Similar to transcranial motor evoked potentials (MEPs) for limb monitoring, coMEPs inform surgical decision making, particularly in eloquent areas such as the brainstem.5 With free-running EMG, the feedback signal relies on irritation of the nerve. Therefore a severed nerve may be indistinguishable from a healthy nerve, due to the lack of signal produced. With triggered EMG, neural injury can only be detected if stimulating proximal to the site of injury (Figure 2). Therefore, false negatives are a significant issue as the signal from a nerve distal to the site of injury is identical to a healthy nerve. The strength of coMEPs lies in their ability to monitor the entire pathway, allowing them to capture the decrease in nerve signal proportional to the extent of pathway injury at any point.

Since their introduction, coMEPs have been expanded for monitoring of CNs V, VII, IX, X, XI, and XII, although widespread adoption has been limited by surgeon experience and inconsistent outcomes. We hypothesize that these inconsistencies are largely due to variations in technical implementation. This study reviews the current use of coMEPs in skull base surgery, their evolving applications, technical variations, and future potential.

## METHODS

### Study Selection

We conducted a systematic review using Covidence to include all articles reporting coMEP neuromonitoring published in Pubmed, Embase, and the Web of Science from inception through December 6, 2023 using the following search terms: [corticobulbar OR (cranial AND nerve*) OR (facial AND nerve) OR (oculomotor AND nerve) OR (mandibular AND nerve) OR (vagus AND nerve) OR (accessory AND nerve) OR (spinal AND accessory AND nerve) OR (glossopharyngeal AND nerve)] AND [motor AND evoked AND potential* OR (“motor evoked” AND potential) OR MEP OR cbMEP OR coMEP] AND (operative OR surgery OR neurosurgery). Articles were included in the analysis if they reported any application of coMEP for monitoring of any CN for any cranial or cervical spine pathology and described electrode placement, nerves and muscles studied, and stimulation parameters used. Multiple study designs were permitted, including randomized controlled trials, case-control, cohort, cross-sectional, case series, and case reports. Studies not available in English, animal studies, nonoriginal investigations (reviews, editorials, letters), investigations in which only abstracts were available, and nonpeer reviewed materials were excluded. Each article was manually screened by at least 2 of 4 independent reviewers (C.A.J., R.V.P., M.B., T.M.) in 2 rounds: first by abstracts, then by full text (Figure 3). Discrepancies were resolved by a third reviewer (W.L.B.). This study adhered to the 2020 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines for systematic reviews. This study was not registered and no protocol was prepared.

*FIGURE 3.: Preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses study selection flow diagram. Flow diagram depicting the process of study identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and final inclusion in the qualitative synthesis.*

### Data Extraction

Our primary outcomes of interest included methodology of implementation as well as sensitivity and specificity of the neuromonitoring modality. We extracted data on study design, country of investigation, pathology, patient age range, and the number of cases using coMEPs. We also recorded the terminology used for coMEPs in each study, as well as the CNs and muscles monitored, and comparative data with other neuromonitoring modalities. Technical data regarding stimulation methods (electrode placement, type of electrodes, whether the electrodes were insulated or noninsulated), stimulation parameters (type, filter settings, pulse duration, train length, interstimulus interval, constant current or constant voltage, and the use of fixed or variable parameters), method of artifact detection, double train application and timing, and equipment used were documented. Anesthetic use, outcome measures, and follow-up time were collected when available, including intraoperative responses, postoperative function, amplitude decrease to deficit, sensitivity, specificity, monitorability rate (defined as proportion of patients in whom an interpretable coMEP signal could be recorded at baseline), and false-positive/negative rates. Studies that did not include clear reporting of CNs monitored or outcome measures were not included in the quantitative synthesis of metrics.

### Statistical Analysis

We analyzed aggregate data to assess the incidence, reporting variability, and sensitivity/specificity of coMEPs. Statistical analysis and data visualization were conducted using Excel v16.103.2 (Microsoft Excel) and R version 4.3.2, R studio 2024.12.0 (The R Foundation).

## RESULTS

### Evolution of coMEPs

Experience with coMEPs has grown in the 2 decades since its introduction for facial nerve monitoring (Figure 4A). Reflective of its origins, the most common coMEP application was in cerebellopontine angle surgeries, primarily for vestibular schwannoma (37/72 studies, 52%), followed by microvascular decompression (MVD) and other skull base pathologies (Figure 4B). Only 4% of studies focused on brainstem pathologies, with the remaining 18% not specified or including other pathologies not otherwise categorized.

Of 3078 cases using corticobulbar MEPs, reported in 72 studies from 2005 to 2023 (Table 1), at least 2711 were unique, with the remaining 367 cases from groups with multiple publications that could not be verified as distinct. Most studies (91.7%) were case reports or case series (median 26 cases, range 1-367 cases) (Figure 4C), and only one study identified was prospectively designed. coMEP studies largely came from a small group of select countries, led by Japan (25%), followed by China (11.1%), the US (9.7%) and Germany (9.7%) (Figure 4D). A minority of studies (13.9%, n = 10) included pediatric patients (younger than18 years), and only one focused exclusively on this group. The facial nerve was the most commonly analyzed (included in 70.8% of studies, and the exclusive focus of 56.9% of studies), followed by the vagus nerve (included in 27.8% of studies, exclusive focus of 12.5% of studies), with a small number focusing on hypoglossal and glossopharyngeal pathways, indicating incipient experience in the field (Figure 4E). Studies monitored up to 6 CNs concurrently, with the majority monitoring just a single nerve (Figure 5A). Most CNs were monitored by a single muscle, although studies of the facial nerve frequently monitored 2 to 3 muscles, with some studies monitoring up to 5 (Figure 5B).

Correlation of monitoring changes to clinically significant deficits was inconsistently reported. In all, 81.9% of studies (59/72) reported clinical outcomes, of which 48 studies reported some new postoperative deficit. Forty-four studies reported some deficits correlating with monitoring changes, and 27 reported some deficits that did not correlate with monitoring changes. Thirty-three studies reported changes in monitoring that did not result in a new postoperative deficit. Four studies reported no change in intraoperative coMEP corresponding to no postoperative deficits.

Follow-up varied widely, with 77.8% (56 studies) reporting follow-up, ranging from 0 to 30 months (average 6.6 months). Of these, 35 studies included multiple follow-up time points, whereas 18 reported only immediate postoperative follow-up or follow-up of unclear timing, and 3 studies reported just one delayed time point. The second follow-up ranged from discharge or 1 to 2 weeks postoperative up to 30 months.

Signal changes, reported in 26/41 of studies focused on the facial nerve, were measured in different ways across studies. The most common harbinger of facial nerve injury was amplitude reduction (18 studies), with alert criteria ranging from 30% to 75% decrease. Other indicators included increased stimulation thresholds (5 studies) and changes in the final-to-baseline ratio (3 studies). Of those 18 studies that relied on amplitude changes, a majority (61%, n = 11) applied a 50% amplitude decrease threshold to signal postoperative deficit.

Nearly all studies used at least one other modality of facial nerve monitoring (90.2%, 37/41), most of which included facial nerve EMG, in addition to coMEPs (68.3%, 28/41). However, only 24.4% (10/41) of studies used a direct comparator group, most frequently lateral spread response (4/10) or the blink reflex (3/10). Notably, lateral spread response was used only in studies of MVD for hemifacial spasm. Of the 26 studies reporting coMEP changes, 6 compared coMEP changes with traditional IONM changes associated with facial nerve injury.

Specificity or sensitivity was reported in less than half of the monitoring studies focused on the facial nerve (20/41). For orbicularis oris, sensitivity ranged from 53.8% to 100% (median 82.0%, IQR 67.25-90.5)3,4,11,13,16,31,47 and specificity ranged from 60% to 89.7% (median 84%, IQR 70.83-88.93).3,4,11,13,16,31,40,47 Median orbicularis oculi sensitivity was 41.7% (IQR 40.85-53.6),13,14,47 with higher specificity (median 93.15%, IQR 90.48-95.5).13,14,40,47 Mentalis sensitivity (91.3%) and specificity (98.6%) were reported in only one study.27 Median combined sensitivity and specificity for multiple facial muscles (orbicularis oris, oculi, mentalis, and nasalis) was 82.9% (IQR 69.83-97.25) and 82.0% (IQR 78.0-99.0), respectively (Figure 6).7,10,28,36-38,45,54,55 Median monitorability was 94% (IQR 87.0-100) across the 26 studies that reported.

### Vagus Nerve Monitoring With Corticobulbar MEPs

Nine studies focused on vagus nerve (CN X) coMEP monitoring, comprising 171 cases. The majority were for intracranial pathologies, predominantly skull base and brainstem conditions. Vagal coMEPs were also commonly applied for extracranial thyroid operations (67/171 cases, 2 studies). Vagal nerve function was assessed by monitoring the vocalis (5 studies) or cricothyroid (3 studies) muscles, or both (1 study), and was not specified in one study. Concurrent monitoring with the laryngeal adductor reflex was reported in 30% of studies.

### Anesthetic Approach

Most of the included studies (70.8%, 51/72) report a total intravenous anesthetic approach, predominantly consisting of propofol with additional intravenous narcotic medications. These agents have mild to moderate, dose-dependent effects on MEP monitoring and are viewed as the standard-of-care anesthetic approach during motor monitoring.76 Seven studies (9.7%, 7/72), however, report the addition of an inhaled halogenated anesthetic to this regimen,14,15,19,24,46,50,60 whereas 2 report administration of nitrous oxide.41,64 These agents produce marked depression of MEP signals, and thus, their confounding effect must be considered when interpreting the associated studies.76 Twelve studies do not report the anesthetic regimen used, and interpretation of these results should be contextualized in the absence of these data.6,11,13,26,30,33,37,38,43,58,59,63 Regarding neuromuscular blocking agents, only one study reported the use of paralytic beyond induction,71 which may potentially confound observed signals.

### Technical Variations in coMEP Methodology

Technical practices varied widely, from electrode placement, to electrode type, to stimulation parameters. Stimulating electrodes on the scalp were placed hemispherically (50/72 studies) more than interhemispherically (14/72 studies), with the cathode at Cz and the anode at C3 (left) or C4 (right). Placement was not specified in 8 studies. For studies of the facial nerve specifically, electrode placement was mostly hemispheric (85.3%, 35/41), with 4 studies using interhemispheric placement (9.8%), 1 study using both (2.4%), and 1 study which did not report stimulating montage (2.4%). In studies of the facial nerve, corkscrew electrodes were used most often for stimulation (75.6%, 31/41), with several studies using subdermal needles (9.8%, 4/41), one study using PEG electrodes (2.4%), and 4 studies in which stimulating electrode choice was not reported (9.8%) (Figure 7A). Orbicularis oris and orbicularis oculi were the most commonly selected muscles for monitoring of the facial nerve (Figure 7B).

Reported pulse width ranged from 50 to 500 microseconds, and train lengths varied from 1 to 8 pulses, with 5 pulses being most common (Figure 8A). The stimulation paradigm applied constant voltage in 41/72 studies, and constant current in 23/72 studies overall, and for studies of just the facial nerve, constant voltage was used in 26/41 and constant current in 12/41. The choice of constant current or constant voltage stimulation varied by equipment used (Figure 8B). Inomed (Inomed Inc.) and Nihon Kohden (Nihon Kohden Corporation) equipment were associated with constant current protocols; Cadwell (Cadwell Industries, Inc.), Natus, and Nicolet (Natus Medical Incorporated) equipment were associated with constant voltage; and Axon (Axon Systems) and Medtronic (Medtronic) used both paradigms.

Artifact detection as a metric of coMEP reliability also varied in practice. Single pulse response was the most common metric of false-negative direct transmission of calvarial electrical stimulation to the peripheral muscles instead of through brain neural pathways. Peripheral response was noted in two-thirds (65.9%, 27/41) of studies of facial nerve monitoring and one-third of studies (31.3%, 5/16) assessing lower CN coMEPs. Strikingly, the method of delivering and measuring the peripheral single pulse response also varied widely across the facial nerve literature, with a double train delivered in only 34.1% (14/41) of studies (not delivered in 24.4% and not reported in 41.5%), and the timing of pulse delivery ranging from 40 ms before to 90 ms after the primary train (Figure 8C). Latency also functioned as a metric of artifact detection, with shorter latencies (<10 ms) being attributed to activation of the facial nerve by extracranial current spread, and was used in another 12.2% of studies (5/41).

## DISCUSSION

Corticobulbar MEPs are rapidly broadening in adoption, from their original application for facial nerve monitoring during vestibular schwannoma surgery. However, widespread adoption remains limited by significant variation in methodology and inconsistent correlation with outcome. We present an in-depth review of operative uses, limitations, and opportunities for improvement.

Practice patterns in coMEP monitoring technique varied in almost every detail. This included the type and number of muscles monitored, electrode type and placement, stimulus parameters, and artifact detection techniques. Unsurprisingly, these methodological variations contribute to heterogeneity in results achieved. Less than half of facial nerve studies quantified monitoring accuracy, and those that did showed wide discrepancies due to technical differences. Peripheral response artifacts, typically assessed through the presence or absence of a single pulse response, were inconsistently captured in addition to being delivered and measured in different ways. Latency was also used as an alternative method to identify artifacts of extracranial stimulation. Most of the facial nerve studies used hemispheric scalp electrode placement, which has been demonstrated to be more reliable for CN VII responses. In comparison, studies examining vagal coMEPs favor interhemispheric stimulation over hemispheric stimulation.34,61 Notably, the choice between constant current and constant voltage stimulation depended on the equipment used, although this did not seem to affect outcomes.

Variability in sensitivity and specificity of different muscles further complicates the reliability of coMEP data.13,40,47 Previous studies have contended that orbicularis oris recording tends to be more reliable than orbicularis oculi because of reduced susceptibility to peripheral artifact, although we did not find that to be substantiated in our aggregate data.13,40,47 Moreover, in our review, only 65.9% of facial nerve studies and 31.3% of lower CN studies used single pulse responses to control for peripheral stimulation. Susceptibility to artifact could be mitigated by monitoring multiple muscle groups, which is uncommon across practices because most of the studies focused on facial nerve coMEPs monitored only one (24.4%) or 2 (31.7%) muscles. Monitoring more muscles on a regular basis could improve coMEP reliability.

Reporting of clinical follow-up and outcome, whether immediate or delayed, was also inconsistent. Nearly a quarter of studies reported no follow-up, and 18% lacked outcome measures, often because of their technical focus. This makes it difficult to interpret the long-term predictive value of coMEPs, as immediate postoperative deficits may not reflect permanent damage. Furthermore, although 90.2% of studies of the facial nerve reported using other monitoring modalities alongside coMEPs, less than a quarter of those studies directly compared coMEPs with alternative techniques, leaving a gap in understanding its relative merits. Future studies including immediate and long-term outcomes may better guide the predictive accuracy of coMEPs and improve clinical decision making.

Despite these methodological challenges, coMEPs are associated with improved preservation of facial nerve integrity,60 and prediction of outcome.13 A meta-analysis of stringently selected studies reported sensitivity (0.81) and specificity (0.94) for coMEPs as a measure of facial nerve function in cerebellopontine angle tumor surgery,77 which exceeded the averages found in our review. Importantly, they noted that sensitivity and specificity across studies has improved over time, likely because of refinements in technique. However, some studies suggest that coMEPs may not always influence patient outcomes, despite its accuracy in predicting facial nerve function, potentially due to inconsistencies in how intraoperative data are used by the surgical team.11 Although many studies cite a 50% decrease in amplitude as indicative of potential nerve damage,4,11,39,40,77 there is no consensus on a standardized alert threshold. Establishing clear, evidence-based criteria for intraoperative alert will be essential for coMEPs to transition from a purely predictive tool to a preventative one, enabling earlier intervention and potentially improving patient outcomes.

We found that 43% of studies have expanded to include or focus on CNs other than the facial nerve, signaling growing interest in broadening utilization of coMEPs. This trend is reflected in the heterogeneous terminology used to refer to coMEPs, including “PharyngealMEPs”, “facial motor evoked potentials”, and “VagalMEPs”, indicating the diverse ways coMEPs are being applied. In addition to monitoring during tumor resections, coMEPs are increasingly used in MVD for trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, and even hemilingual spasm.21,57,69 Nonetheless, the overall number of cases being monitored with coMEPs remains small, with most studies reporting fewer than 100 cases.

coMEP monitoring remains underused in pediatric populations, with only 13.9% of studies including children. Interestingly, a pediatric-specific study found that coMEP thresholds in children were similar to those reported in adults, suggesting that coMEPs can be safely and effectively used in pediatric patients without modification.28 This represents a significant area of potential growth in coMEP application, given the enrichment of posterior fossa and brainstem pathologies in the pediatric population.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in medical research and innovation and is well positioned to augment pattern recognition in IONM, while improving access to and standardization of these tools. Emerging studies demonstrate the feasibility of neural network-based MEP detection and the use of AI to identify clinically meaningful signal features that enhance accuracy and reliability, in addition to furthering research in the field.78,79 Continued, iterative integration of AI into signal acquisition, quality control, and interpretation has the potential to strengthen performance and accelerate broader adoption of advanced IONM platforms.

We have summarized our findings of the most commonly used approaches and techniques, as well as our recommendations for optimal performance of coMEP monitoring in Table 2. In an effort to increase transparency and consistency, we have created a recommended reporting checklist for future coMEP studies to facilitate standardized high quality data reporting in future publications (Table 3). Continuing to aggregate and analyze our collective experience with this technique is critical to increasing implementation and reliability.

### Limitations

Our study has several limitations, primarily due to the inherent constraints of systematic reviews. Variability in study design, reporting practices, and data quality made direct comparisons difficult. Although we aimed to capture the full scope of coMEP applications, many studies lacked detailed follow-up or quantitative data. Owing to the heterogeneity in the data, we have reported median values and interquartile ranges to reflect observed ranges and distributions. These values do not constitute pooled estimates. Nearly all studies were retrospective in design. Given the lack of prospective data, conclusions regarding impact on outcomes remains limited.

## CONCLUSION

coMEP monitoring offers significant potential to improve the continuous monitoring of CN pathways during surgery. Refinement of techniques is needed to achieve improved accuracy and reliability, standardized alert criteria, and enhanced consistency for artifact detection. The field would benefit from standardization of methodologies and more consistent clinical outcome reporting to encourage increased utilization and fully realize the potential of coMEPs in neurosurgery.

## Abstract

Alterations to the excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratio are postulated to underlie behavioral phenotypes in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) patients and mouse models. However, in wild type mice the E/I ratio is not constant, but instead oscillates across the 24-h day. Therefore, we tested whether E/I regulation, rather than the overall E/I ratio, is disrupted in two ASD-related mouse lines: Fmr1 KO and BTBR, models of syndromic and idiopathic ASD, respectively. The E/I ratio is dysregulated in both models, but in different ways: the oscillation is lost in Fmr1 KO and reversed in BTBR mice. Phenotypes in both models associate with differences the timing of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission and endocannabinoid signaling compared to wild type mice, but not with altered sleep. These findings raise the possibility that ASD-related phenotypes may be produced by a mismatch between E/I and behavioral state, rather than alterations to overall E/I levels per se.

## Introduction

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder estimated to affect 1 in 39 children.1 The core features of ASD are language deficits, social interaction deficits, and repetitive or restrictive behaviors and interests. These features are accompanied by sensory abnormalities in >90% of cases, and sensory processing differences have been reported to affect every sensory modality.2,3 The visual system in particular is of great interest, as behavioral deficits have been tied to altered processing in the primary visual cortex (V1) of Fmr1 knockout (KO) mice.4 Moreover, a recent analysis in humans concluded that regarding alterations in gene expression, “the primary visual cortex is the most affected region in ASD”.5

ASD is genetically diverse, but elevation of the ratio between excitatory and inhibitory signaling (E/I ratio) in the brain has been proposed as a unifying mechanism.6 Accordingly, higher E/I ratio and/or lower inhibition has been observed in sensory cortices of many ASD mouse models.7,8,9,10,11,12,13,14,15 However, the opposite (decreased E/I ratio, increased inhibition, and/or decreased excitation) has also been reported.16,17,18,19,20,21

One possible explanation for these opposing findings is that regulation of the E/I ratio, rather than the E/I ratio itself, is disrupted in ASD. In wild type (WT) mice, the E/I ratio in primary visual cortex (V1) changes over the course of the 24-h light:dark cycle, such that it is low during the light (rest) phase.22 Therefore, an apparent elevation of the E/I ratio in ASD models could either be due to an increased E/I at all times of day or a dysregulated (e.g., flattened or phase-shifted) E/I oscillation. However, studies that measure the E/I ratio a single time of day cannot distinguish between these possibilities.

These considerations prompted us to examine possible E/I ratio dysregulation in two ASD-related mouse models with disparate genetic causes: the Fmr1 knockout (Fmr1 KO) mouse, which models Fragile X syndrome,23 the most frequent monogenic cause of intellectual disability and ASD in humans,24 and the BTBR T + Itpr3tf/J (BTBR) mouse, an inbred line that models idiopathic ASD.25,26 We show that the E/I ratio is dysregulated in both Fmr1 KO and BTBR mice but in different ways: the oscillation is flattened in Fmr1 KO mice and the timing of the oscillation is reversed in BTBR mice. Differences in endocannabinoid (eCB) signaling, but not sleep architecture, correspond to the patterns of E/I dysregulation in both lines, suggesting that eCB disruption could be a common feature across genetically diverse forms of ASD.

## Results

### The E/I ratio is dysregulated in two mouse models of ASD

We first determined whether the E/I ratio is dysregulated across the 24-h light/dark cycle in Fmr1 KO mice. We measured the E/I ratio by electrically stimulating in V1 layer 2/3 and recording excitatory and inhibitory synaptic responses in pyramidal cells lateral to the stimulating electrode (Figure 1A). We initially measured E/I in slices obtained from animals killed at two different time points: ZT0 and ZT12. As expected, in WT controls, the E/I ratio was higher at ZT0 (t(51) = 3.92, p = 0.0003, unpaired t test). In contrast, the E/I ratio in Fmr1 KO animals was not different between ZT0 and ZT12 (U = 312, p = 0.22, Mann-Whitney U test), consistent with E/I dysregulation. To distinguish between a flattening vs. altered timing of the E/I oscillation, we then included additional time points (ZT6, 18; Figure 1A). While the E/I ratio in Fmr1 WT animals was higher when the animal had been in the dark phase (ZT0, 18), there was no time of day effect in Fmr1 KO animals, indicating that the E/I oscillation is flattened (Figure 1B).

To directly compare between genotypes, we conducted a two-way ANOVA with time of day and genotype as main factors. We previously showed that the E/I ratio becomes stable within 4h of light/dark phase transitions, consistent with our current findings in Fmr1 WT mice22; Figure 1). Therefore, for each genotype, data were pooled into dark (ZT0, 18) and light (ZT6, 12) phase groups. There was a significant interaction between genotype and time of day but no main genotype effect (Table S1), confirming that E/I regulation, rather than overall magnitude, is altered in Fmr1 KO mice. Post-hoc analysis revealed that the E/I ratio was significantly lower in the dark phase (p = 0.003, Holm-Sidak test) but not significantly higher in the light phase (p = 0.18) in Fmr1 KO mice, indicating that the E/I oscillation flattening is predominantly carried by a decrease in the dark phase.

We then examined the E/I oscillation in BTBR and C57Bl/6J (B6) control mice (Figure 1A). As expected, B6 controls exhibited a higher E/I ratio at ZT0 than at ZT12 (Figure 1C). In contrast, the E/I ratio in the BTBR mice followed the opposite pattern, with a higher E/I ratio at ZT12 than ZT0 (Figure 1C). This indicates that the E/I ratio oscillates, but with reversed timing, in BTBR mice. A two-way ANOVA revealed an interaction between genotype and time of day but no main effect of genotype (Table S1), demonstrating that regulation of the E/I oscillation, rather than overall magnitude, is altered in BTBR mice. Post-hoc analysis showed that, compared to B6 controls, BTBR mice had a significantly lower E/I ratio at ZT0 (p = 0.001, Holm-Sidak test) and higher E/I ratio at ZT12 (p = 0.03), consistent with reversal of the E/I oscillation.

We wished to confirm that V1 circuit function was otherwise normal in these lines. The E/I ratio oscillates over the 24-h day in the lateral (layer 2/3-2/3) circuit, but not in the feedforward (layer 4-2/3) circuit in V1 of WT mice.22 To confirm that Fmr1 KO and BTBR mice did not display an abnormal oscillation in this circuit, we electrically stimulated layer 4 while recording synaptic currents in layer 2/3 of V1 slices. We confirmed that the E/I ratio did not change across the day for Fmr1 KO, Fmr1 WT, BTBR, or B6 animals (Figure S1). In contrast with primary somatosensory cortex (S1),7 there was no main effect of genotype for either ASD model in the layer 4-2/3 circuit of V1 (Figure S1 and Table S1). Mean ± SEM E/I ratio values for all experiments are presented in Table S2.

Additionally, V1 area is reduced in BTBR mice,27 raising the concern that V1 may be fundamentally disorganized, or that visual input may not reach the cortex. Using optical imaging in vivo, we confirmed that V1, although smaller, is responsive to visual input and expresses ocular dominance bias and retinotopy comparable to B6 mice (Figure S2). Fmr1 KO mice are normal in these respects (Figure S2). These results suggest that the E/I ratio phenotypes we observed are not due to a general disruption of circuitry in the visual pathway.

### Altered sleep timing does not explain E/I dysregulation in two mouse models of ASD

Sleep regulates the oscillation of both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission over the course of the day.22,28 Therefore, it is possible that the observed E/I dysregulation in Fmr1 KO and BTBR mice is due to abnormal sleep timing. Indeed, decreased sleep and altered sleep bout duration and frequency during the light phase have been reported in Fmr1 KO mice.29,30,31 We therefore continuously recorded EEG and EMG signals in the home cage using wireless telemetry for three days.

Sleep timing and architecture was grossly normal in Fmr1 KO and BTBR mice compared to WT controls. Overall amounts of wake, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, and REM sleep did not differ between Fmr1 KO and WT or between BTBR and B6 mice (Figure S3 and Table S3). We did not replicate the NREM or REM sleep deficits reported in Fmr1 KO mice,30,31 possibly due to an emergence of these deficits with age.29 Furthermore, the distribution of time spent in each state across the day did not differ between Fmr1 KO and WT mice (Figure 2A). The overall pattern of sleep timing appeared normal in BTBR mice, but there was a significant interaction between genotype and time of day for wake and REM amounts (Figure 2B and Table S3). However, these slight differences cannot explain the reversal of the E/I oscillation in BTBR mice, since BTBR mice slept primarily during the light phase.

### eCB signaling is dysregulated in Fmr1 KO and BTBR mice

Multiple mechanisms can potentially affect the E/I ratio (see discussion). Among them, we previously identified eCB signaling as one candidate mechanism contributing to time-of-day-dependent E/I changes in WT mice.22 This raises the possibility that eCB signaling is altered in Fmr1 KO and BTBR mice. In support of this idea, behavioral phenotypes in both lines can be normalized by pharmacological manipulation of eCB signaling.37 Therefore, we tested whether the time-of-day-specific sensitivity of inhibitory transmission to the eCB receptor agonist (+)-WIN 55,212-2 (WIN) is altered in each line. As previously, we evaluated the effects of WIN on spontaneous inhibitory currents (sIPSCs) because under standard slice recording conditions the agonist only affects GABA responses evoked by action potentials,38 not mIPSCs. In WT mice, WIN suppresses sIPSCs when endogenous eCB levels are low (ZT12), and this effect is occluded when endogenous eCB levels are high (ZT0) (Bridi et al., 2020; Figure 5). In contrast, both Fmr1 KO and BTBR mice showed altered patterns of WIN sensitivity. In Fmr1 KO mice, WIN reduced sIPSCs at both times of day (Figure 5A). In BTBR mice, WIN suppressed sIPSCs when inhibition is abnormally high (ZT0) but this effect was occluded when inhibition was already low (ZT12) (Figure 5B). Repeating this experiment using an eCB receptor antagonist (SR141716A, SR) yielded complementary results (Figure S4). Together, these results are consistent with flattening and reversal of the evoked E/I balance in Fmr1 KO and BTBR mice, respectively, that is driven in part by altered eCB signaling (Figure 6). We also note that additional mechanisms might regulate the daily modulation of mIPSCs.
